questions.prompt: What is an op-amp's slew rate (SR)?
options: The maximum rate of change of the output voltage, \(SR=\left.\dfrac{dV_o}{dt}\right|_{max}\), usually quoted in \(\mathrm{V/\mu s}\)
The frequency at which the gain falls to 1
The time the output takes to settle within 1%
The maximum output voltage swing
questions.explanation:
Reader Eq. 18.17. However the input moves, the output can't change faster than SR; for big, fast signals the output becomes a straight ramp of slope SR (the 'slew-limited region' in the figure).
• The unity-gain frequency is a LINEAR (small-signal) limit.
• Settling time and swing are different specs.

questions.prompt: An op-amp with \(SR=10\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\) must make a 5 V output step. Ignoring the final exponential settling, how long does the slew-limited ramp take, in µs?
questions.explanation:
A ramp at constant slope: \(t=\dfrac{\Delta V}{SR}=\dfrac{5\ \mathrm{V}}{10\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}}=0.5\ \mu\mathrm{s}\).
Common mistake: multiplying instead of dividing (50 µs).

questions.prompt: How does slew-rate limiting differ from a bandwidth limit for a large sine wave?
options: They are the same effect described in two ways
A bandwidth limit distorts the sine; slewing only delays it
Slewing affects only small signals
Slewing is NONLINEAR (the sine is distorted toward a triangle); a bandwidth limit is linear (a sine stays a sine, just smaller and phase-shifted)
questions.explanation:
Reader Sec. 18.4.2: the finite bandwidth is a linear phenomenon and preserves the sinusoidal shape. Slewing caps the slope, so the steep parts of the sine are replaced by straight ramps (harmonics appear). It depends on amplitude; a bandwidth limit doesn't.
• Slewing is a LARGE-signal effect.
questions.figure_alt: A dashed ideal sine wave and a solid output waveform whose steep parts are replaced by straight ramps, looking triangular.

questions.prompt: An op-amp has \(SR=1\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\) and a rated maximum output of \(V_{o,max}=10\ \mathrm{V}\) peak. What is its full-power bandwidth \(f_{max}=\dfrac{SR}{2\pi V_{o,max}}\), in kHz?
questions.explanation:
A sine \(V\sin\omega t\) has maximum slope \(V\omega\) (reader Eq. 18.26). Setting \(2\pi f V=SR\): \(f_{max}=\dfrac{10^6\ \mathrm{V/s}}{2\pi\times10\ \mathrm{V}}=15.92\ \mathrm{kHz}\) (Eq. 18.28).
Common mistakes: forgetting \(2\pi\) (100 kHz) or using \(\mathrm{V/\mu s}\) as \(\mathrm{V/s}\).

questions.prompt: An op-amp with \(SR=5\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\) must output a 200 kHz sine without slewing. What is the largest peak amplitude it can deliver, in V?
questions.explanation:
Require \(V_p\,\omega\le SR\): \(V_p\le\dfrac{SR}{2\pi f}=\dfrac{5\times10^6}{2\pi\times2\times10^5}=3.979\ \mathrm{V}\).
Above this amplitude the waveform turns triangular even though 200 kHz may be far below the op-amp's bandwidth.

questions.prompt: A sine wave far above the full-power bandwidth is applied at large amplitude to a follower. What does the output look like?
options: A clean sine, just phase-shifted
A square wave at the supply rails
Close to a triangle wave, with slopes \(\pm SR\), and smaller than the ideal amplitude
A clean sine of the full amplitude, delayed by \(1/SR\)
questions.explanation:
When the required slope \(V\omega\) far exceeds SR, the output spends almost all its time ramping at \(+SR\) or \(-SR\): a triangle whose amplitude is limited to about \(\dfrac{SR\cdot T}{4}\). That is non-sinusoidal distortion (reader Fig. 18.17).
• Rails clip in voltage, not in slope.
questions.figure_alt: Ideal sine and a triangle-like slew-limited output.

questions.prompt: A follower uses an op-amp with \(SR=0.5\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\) and \(f_u=1\ \mathrm{MHz}\). What is the largest input step that settles linearly (no slewing at all), in mV?
questions.explanation:
The linear response \(V(1-e^{-\omega_ut})\) starts with slope \(V\omega_u\) (reader Eq. 18.20–18.21). No slewing requires \(V\omega_u<SR\):
\[V<\dfrac{SR}{\omega_u}=\dfrac{5\times10^5}{2\pi\times10^6}=79.58\ \mathrm{mV}\]
Gotcha: even a sub-0.1 V step can slew in a fast op-amp. 'Large signal' is relative to \(SR/\omega_u\), not to the supply.
questions.figure_alt: Small step and an exponential response.

questions.prompt: An op-amp (\(f_u=1\ \mathrm{MHz}\), \(SR=0.5\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\)) is used in a gain-10 non-inverting amplifier. A 0.1 V input step makes a 1 V output step. Does it slew?
options: No: the input step is only 0.1 V
Yes: the closed-loop bandwidth is \(f_u/10\), so the linear initial slope is \(1\ \mathrm{V}\times2\pi\times100\ \mathrm{kHz}=0.63\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}>SR\)
No: higher gain means a slower amplifier, which can't slew
Yes, and its slope is 10 times larger than for a 0.1 V step in a follower
questions.explanation:
Output slope \(=V_{o,step}\,\omega_0=(10\times0.1)\times\dfrac{\omega_u}{10}=0.1\times\omega_u=0.63\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\). The gain multiplies the step but divides the bandwidth by the same factor, so the initial slope equals the follower's with the same INPUT step. It exceeds 0.5 V/µs, so the output slews.
Gotcha: higher gain doesn't protect you from slewing.

questions.prompt: A follower uses an op-amp with \(SR=10\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\) and \(f_u=1\ \mathrm{MHz}\). A 1 V-peak, 1 MHz sine is applied. What is the output?
options: A sine of about 0.71 V peak, lagging \(45^\circ\): bandwidth-limited, not slew-limited (it needs only \(6.3\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\))
A triangle wave, because 1 MHz is too fast
A 1 V-peak sine, unaffected
A sine of about 0.5 V peak due to slewing
questions.explanation:
Slope needed: \(V\omega=2\pi\times10^6\times1=6.3\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}<10\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\), so no slewing. But 1 MHz is the follower's \(-3\ \mathrm{dB}\) frequency (\(f_u\)), so the LINEAR response is \(1/\sqrt2\approx0.71\) of the input with \(-45^\circ\) phase.
Gotcha: check both limits; here the linear one bites first.

questions.prompt: Preview of datasheets. The ADA4891 (reader Sec. 18.6) has \(SR=170\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\). For a 2 V-peak output sine, what is its full-power bandwidth, in MHz?
questions.explanation:
\(f_{max}=\dfrac{SR}{2\pi V}=\dfrac{1.7\times10^8}{2\pi\times2}=13.53\ \mathrm{MHz}\).
Its GBW is 240 MHz, but a 2 V-peak sine distorts above ~13.5 MHz: datasheets list both because either can be the limit.

questions.prompt: Preview of datasheets. An audio amplifier stage must deliver 10 V peak at 20 kHz without slewing. What minimum slew rate must you look for on the datasheet, in \(\mathrm{V/\mu s}\)?
questions.explanation:
\(SR_{min}=2\pi fV=2\pi\times2\times10^4\times10=1.257\times10^6\ \mathrm{V/s}=1.257\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\).
In practice designers add margin (2–5×). A classic 0.5 V/µs part would distort here.

questions.prompt: Preview of datasheets. You need a gain of 10 delivering a 1 MHz sine of 5 V peak. Which op-amp (GBW, SR) meets both the bandwidth and the slew requirement?
options: GBW 10 MHz, SR 5 V/µs
GBW 1 MHz, SR 50 V/µs
GBW 3 MHz, SR 0.5 V/µs
GBW 240 MHz, SR 170 V/µs
questions.explanation:
Bandwidth: gain 10 needs GBW well above \(10\times1\ \mathrm{MHz}=10\ \mathrm{MHz}\). Slew: \(2\pi\times10^6\times5=31.4\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\).
• GBW 10 MHz puts 1 MHz right at the \(-3\) dB point, and 5 V/µs slews badly.
• GBW 1 MHz gives only 100 kHz bandwidth at gain 10.
• GBW 3 MHz and 0.5 V/µs fail both.
Only the 240 MHz / 170 V/µs part passes both.
